          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
CONMT.PET.(C) No. 877/2025 in C.A. No. 14604/2024 
1. In pursuance of our last order dated 14.7.2026, a fresh
status report has been placed before us in the form of an
affidavit, duly affirmed by P. Guruprasad, Chairman, U.P. Awas
Evam Vikas Parishad, highlighting what steps have been taken
after 14.7.2026.
2. The report talks about (i) action taken in respect of 44
sealed  properties;  (ii)  status  of  removal/demolition  of
unauthorised  constructions  in  setback  areas;  (iii)  survey
5

--- Page 57 ---
regarding unauthorised construction at village Uldepur situated
on the outskirts of Meerut; (iv) status of EWS/Lower Income
Group (LIG) properties; and (5) fresh survey regarding illegal
commercial constructions in other areas of Meerut.
3. It appears, on plain reading of the report, that notices
were issued to the respective owners of the 44 properties which
were sealed at the earliest point of time. 20 out of those 44
properties have been demolished, and the unauthorised commercial
use has been discontinued.  The report indicates that, out of 44
properties, 38 properties had building plans sanctioned, but the
owners had put up unauthorised additional construction and the
properties were used for commercial purposes. Six properties
were sold as plots, and unauthorised residential as well as
commercial construction was put up without any sanction of plan
or map approval.
4. We direct the authorities to ensure that the remaining 24
properties, out of 44 on which seals have been applied, be
demolished accordingly at the earliest.
5. We also take notice of the fact that, 201 properties were
in  the  process  of  removal/demolition  of  unauthorised
constructions raised in the mandatory setback areas. Out of 201
properties identified the setback areas of 63 properties have
been  completely  removed/demolished  while  action  for
6

--- Page 58 ---
removal/demolition is presently continuing in respect of the
remaining 138 properties. 
6. Let the above action proceed further expeditiously, and the
authorities shall see to it that the remaining 138 properties,
with unauthorised construction in the setback areas, are also
demolished. 
7. We are shocked and disturbed to learn, reading the status
report, that hundreds of illegal residential colonies have come
up at Uldepur.
8. Uldepur is situated on the outskirts of Meerut.
9. We enquired with Mr. Pahwa, the learned senior counsel
appearing for the Respondent no. 10 whether these illegal
residential colonies at Uldepur have come up on Government land
or land owned by different individuals. According to Mr. Pahwa,
the different parcels of land are owned by individuals, and they
have been purchased by people at large, and these residential
colonies have been constructed without any permission or without
getting any plans sanctioned from the authorities, i.e., namely,
the Meerut Development Authority.
10. In so far as Uldepur is concerned, we are of the firm view
that we should  order a judicial commission to undertake an
extensive inquiry as regards the following:
7

--- Page 59 ---
(i) Whether  these  parcels  of  land  on  which  illegal
residential colonies have been constructed are in the
ownership of the Government?
(ii) If the land does not belong to the Government, then
who all are the lawful owners of these vast parcels
of land?
(iii) If the inquiry reveals that the land does not belong
to the Government but the same belongs to different
individuals, then in what manner transactions took
place between the land-owners and the purchasers?
(iv) Why Meerut Development Authority kept quiet for a
period of more than five years and permitted these
illegal residential colonies to come up before their
very eyes?
(v) Whether the illegal residential colonies have come up
in collusion and connivance with the officials of the
Meerut Development Authority and, if yes, who all are
those officials responsible for the same?
11. We appoint Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia, former
Judge of this Court, to act as the Chairperson of the Judicial
Commission. It shall be within the discretion of the Chairperson
8

--- Page 60 ---
to induct other members in the Commission as he may deem fit for
the smooth, effective and meaningful conduct of the inquiry. The
remit of the Commission shall be the questions which we have
framed as referred to above. It shall be open for the Commission
to probe into any further issue or question that it may deem fit
and appropriate to enquire.
12. In the aforesaid context, we direct that secretariat and
secretarial assistance will be provided by the State of Uttar
Pradesh. The Meerut Development Authority Commissioner, namely,
Shri P. Guruprasad will be the nodal officer to co-ordinate with
Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia. As part of remuneration payable to
Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia and any co-opted member, the State
shall at the first instance, deposit in the Registry of this
court an amount of Rs. 35,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty-Five Lakhs
Only) within a period of one week from today. The amount on
deposit shall be kept in a nationalised bank in a short-term
Fixed Deposit on auto renewal basis.
13. Meanwhile, we direct the authorities to proceed, at the
earliest, to demolish each and every illegal structure put up at
Uldepur as discussed above in more details. 
14.  The  authorities  must  also  ensure  that  effective  and
expeditious disposal of demolition debris is undertaken on a
9

--- Page 61 ---
daily  basis,  so  that  citizens  are  not  subjected  to  any
inconvenience and hardship. 
15. We also take notice of the fact stated in the report that,
in 486 properties, falling within the EWS and LIG category
respectively, commercial activities were being undertaken. The
report indicates that action has been taken to stop all such
commercial activities being undertaken in these 486 properties
which are meant for residential purposes.
16. In  pursuance  of  our  directions  to  undertake
inspection/survey of other parts of Meerut, the report indicates
that Meerut has been divided into four zones, i.e., Zone-A,
Zone-B, Zone-C and Zone-D, respectively. In Zone-A, 16 teams
deputed for the purpose of inspection/survey have identified
16,726 structures to be absolutely illegal/unauthorised. Out of
16,726  structures,  12,907  comprise  of  residential,  874
residential-cum-non-residential,  and  2945  non-residential
constructions. 
17. We direct the authorities to proceed at the earliest to
take  appropriate  action  against  all  these  16,726  illegal
structures in Zone-A. The first step in the process is to ask
the occupants to vacate the premises and to seal all these
premises, i.e., the 16,726  illegal structures. We direct
accordingly. It is possible that some of these structures may be
10

--- Page 62 ---
in a dilapidated condition and may collapse, resulting into
casualties.  We  do  not  want  this  to  happen  at  any  cost.
Therefore, prompt action is necessary. We direct that prompt
action be taken insofar as all the four zones are concerned. We
make it clear that, God forbid, tomorrow if some untoward
incident occurs and innocent lives are lost, the responsible
government officer shall be held personally liable for the same.
18. The report is silent insofar as Zone-B, Zone-C and Zone-D,
respectively, are concerned. We have no idea how many illegal
structures are there in these three zones. On the next date of
hearing, the authority concerned shall give us a comprehensive
report  as  regards  Zone-B,  Zone-C  and  Zone-D  respectively.
However,  since  illegal  construction  in  Zone-A  has  been
identified, appropriate action shall now be taken for demolition
of the same.
19. The overall picture, as reflected from the status report
appears to be extremely grim and serious. The authorities need
to  work  day  and  night  to  demolish  these  unauthorised
constructions. 
20. On the next date of hearing, the Chairman, U.P. Awas Evam
Vikas  Parishad,  shall  file  a  fresh  report  insofar  as
removal/demolition of construction at Uldepur is concerned,
including the steps that shall be taken insofar as Zones-A, B, C
11

--- Page 63 ---
and D, respectively, of the town are concerned. 
21. Mr.  Tushar  Mehta,  the  learned  Solicitor  General  and
Mr. Navin Pahwa, the learned senior counsel appearing for
Respondent no. 10 would submit that insofar as occupants falling
within EWS and LIG are concerned, the Government may consider
rehabilitating  them  at  some  other  place.  That's  for  the
Government to decide how to rehabilitate them. We are concerned
with  demolition  of  each  and  every  illegal
building/structure/shop in the town of Meerut. 
22.  The extent of unauthorised/illegal construction in the
entire town and at the outskirts is now borne out from the
report itself of the authority. The facts and figures stated in
the status report are alarming.
23. We direct that the process of demolition shall continue and
by the next date of hearing a further status report be placed
before us.
24. We are informed by the learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner  that  his  client  is  receiving  threats  of  dire
consequences from different quarters. If that be so, the State
shall ensure that no harm is caused to his life or limb in any
manner. We make it clear that if any individual, be it a public
servant,  elected  representative  or  any  other  official  or
12

--- Page 64 ---
individual, creates any impediment or obstruction in the process
of demolition as directed by us, such person shall be dealt with
by us very strictly in accordance with law.
25. We request Shri P. Guruprasad, Chairman, U.P. Awas Evam
Vikas Parishad to join the proceedings online on the next date
of hearing.
26. List Conmt.Pet.(C) No. 595/2025 alongwith I.A.No.287125 and
287131 of 2026, Conmt.Pet.(C) No. 877/2025, Conmt.Pet.(C) No.
851/2025, Diary No.7071/2026 and Diary No. 71735 of 2025 on
09.12.2026 at 2.00 P.M. 
27. Registry shall forward one copy of this order at the
earliest to Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia, former Judge
of this Court.

Heard  Ms.  Aishwarya  Bhati,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General, Mr. Karan Bharihoke, learned  Amicus  Curiae  and learned
counsel for various respondents.
2. In terms of our order dated 13.08.2026, the Committee has
placed before us a proposal relating to the - “Guidelines for
Organization and Delivery of Intensive Care Services-Time Frames
6

--- Page 71 ---
M.A. NO. 1364/2026
for Compliance”. The same are reproduced hereunder: 
GUIDELINES FOR ORGANIZATION AND DELIVERY OF INTENSIVE CARE
SERVICES1 
TIME FRAMES FOR COMPLIANCE
ICU LEVEL I
INFRASTRUCTURE
S.No. Guideline Clause Remark 
1. 3.1.1 – Location Changing location and size of existing ICU’s, to align with the
Guidelines, requires thorough reassessment of location, need,
design  and  construction.  The  possibility  of  such  redesign  /
relocation affecting immediate functionality of existing ICUs
cannot be ruled out. 
It is suggested that States be allowed  up  to  12  months  for
complying with Guideline 3.1.1. 
2. 3.1.1 – ICU Size
and Infrastructure
3. 3.1.2  –  Beside
Utilities 
The  facilities  mentioned  under  this  Guideline  require  only
procurement. Guideline 3.1.2 ought to be complied with, without
delay, in a maximum period of 3 months. 
 
4. 3.1.2  –
Emergency
Equipment 
The facilities mentioned under this Guideline require procurement
of sophisticated machinery, some of which may require imports.
However, considering the nature of the equipment, Guideline 3.1.2
qua Emergency Equipment requires expeditious compliance. 
It is suggested that the procurement process including issuance of
Purchase / Delivery Orders be completed within a period  of  3
months. 
Further time may be given for the installation of the equipment on
a case to case basis and depending on delivery schedules for the
same. This should however be subject to a maximum period of 3
further months. 
5. 3.1.3  –  Nursing
Station 
Setting up of nursing stations requires setting up of monitors and
setting up infrastructure that may require time. This is also an
infrastructure and design issue. 
It is suggested that States be allowed  up  to  12  months  for
complying with Guideline 3.1.3 as this is actually a subset of
Guideline 3.1.1.

No. 8402/2016 titled as Asit Baran Mondal & Anr. v. Dr. Rita Sinha & Ors. 
7

--- Page 72 ---
M.A. NO. 1364/2026
6. 3.1.4  –  Imaging
Services
The Guidelines require access to Imaging Services that may
require procurement of sophisticated machinery, some of which
may require imports.
It is suggested that the procurement process including issuance of
Purchase / Delivery Orders be completed within a period  of  3
months. 
Further time may be given for the installation of the equipment on
a case to case basis and depending on delivery schedules for the
same. This should however be subject to a maximum period of 3
further months. 
7. 3.1.5  –  Non-
Emergency
Equipment 
Maximum period of 3 months.
8. 3.1.6  -
Laboratory
Services 
Maximum period of 3 months.
9. 3.1.7 - Infection
Control 
Immediate. 
10. 3.1.8 - Additional
Services 
Maximum period of 1 month.
11. 3.1.9 – Safety Immediate.
12. 3.3  –  Desirable
Equipment  &
Services 
By its very nature the Guidelines define these as additional
services which are desirable. No specific time frame is required for
this category. 
HEALTHCARE PERSONNEL
S.No. Guideline Clause Remark 
1. 3.2.1-3.2.3 This Guideline and its sub-clauses, inter alia, requires recruitment
of ICU Specialists, trained MBBS Doctors, Nurses and  other
Allied Healthcare Personnel.  
The deficits in the numbers of the aforesaid three categories of
professionals are systemic and depends on availability of such
personnel for recruitment.
Most States have requested a period of 12 to 24 months  for this
process to be completed. However, the Committee felt that the said
time frame is excessive. 
2. 3.2.4  –
Documentation 
Immediate.
3. 3.2.5 - Audit Immediate. 
Note 1 : The aforesaid timelines may require special modification for certain states and areas

where the facilities are in hilly, remote and / or other areas that require special
consideration. The Hon’ble Court may accordingly make appropriate relaxation for
such facilities. 
Note 2 : Whereas ICU Level 1 Guidelines are mandatory for a facility to be called ICU, it is
not mandatory for any Hospital to have a Level II or Level III ICU. Given the same, it
would be appropriate that the Guidelines qua Level II and Level III ICUs be strictly
enforced and a facility be termed as Level II / Level III only on full compliance. In
such cases, the facility should be categorised as per the level of compliance and
renamed accordingly. “
3. Broadly, we are in agreement with the time frames suggested

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION

PRADESH AND ORS.               ….RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R  
 
1. Heard. 
2. The petitioner, a citizen of Turkmenistan, has 
approached this Court by way of the instant writ 
petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India 
under deeply disturbing circumstances. The 
petitioner is the mother of Ms. Najmudinova 
Muhabbat1 who had travelled to India in February, 
2026. 
3. The dead body of the deceased was recovered on 
21st February, 2026 from an open field falling within 
 
1 hereinafter referred to as “the deceased”. 

--- Page 101 ---
2 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
the limits of Police Station Mawana, District Meerut, 
Uttar Pradesh. The face of the deceased  had been 
mutilated by corrosive chemical and thereafter, the 
body was abandoned in the open field. Information 
regarding discovery of the dead body was provided at 
the police station at about 6:00 PM on 21st February, 
2026 by one Manoj s/o Ved Prakash, in whose field 
the dead body was seen lying . Initial enquiry was 
undertaken by Sub Inspector Smt. Preeti Sharma.  
4. The State has come up with a case that, as there 
were no identifying marks on the body, efforts were 
made to ascertain the identity of the deceased 
through various means including examination of 
phone calls, social media, newspapers etc. but to no 
avail. The preliminary enquiry also revealed that the 
face of the unidentified wom an had been bu rnt and 
appeared to have been corroded by acid to conceal 
her identity.   
5. An FIR bearing Crime No. 80/2026 came to be 
registered on 25 th February, 2026 against unknown 
persons. On the same day, the dead body was 
subjected to post -mortem examination. The post -
mortem report recorded that the body was 
decomposed and the cause of death was opined to be 

--- Page 102 ---
3 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
septicemia due to chronic illness involving multiple 
organs. 
6. At the time of post-mortem examination, viscera 
samples were preserved from the body viz. right thigh 
muscle with skin, one tooth, a piece of sternum bone 
and scalp hair, for the purpose of DNA examination 
in future. The dead body was then handed back to 
the police.  
7. The police officials, thereafter, proceeded to 
cremate the dead body under the belief that the 
deceased was a Hindu.  However, when the report of 
the death attracted media attention , further 
verification was carried out and assistance of a 
representative appointed by the Embassy of 
Turkmenistan was taken, which affirmed that the 
deceased was not an Indian citizen but was, in fact, 
a citizen of Turkmenistan and was identified as Ms. 
Najmudinova Muhabba t i.e., the petitioner’s 
daugther. 
8. The petitioner has set out a case in the writ 
petition that the dead body was recklessly cremated 
as per Hindu rituals and customs without the 
identity of the deceased having been ascertained. It is 
further alleged that neither the family members nor 

--- Page 103 ---
4 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
the next of kin of the deceased, nor the Embassy of 
Turkmenistan were informed before cremation. The 
petitioner has also alleged that the ashes collected 
pursuant to the cremation were retained by the police 
officials.  
9. In the meantime, the investigation proceeded. 
Certain suspected individuals were investigated into 
and the owner of the hotel in which the deceased was 
last seen was arrested during investigation . 
Recoveries were effected and few more accused 
persons were arrested by the police.  This Court has 
been informed that chargesheet has been filed by the 
local police against four accused persons.  
10. Alleging gross negligence in investigation, t he 
petitioner has approached this Court by way of the 
instant writ petition under Article 32 of the 
Constitution of India with the following prayers:  
i. A writ of mandamus directing constitution 
of a Special Investigation Team comprising 
of officers unconnected with the 
investigation conducted thus far to 
conduct a free, fair and independent 
investigation into the C ase Crime No. 

--- Page 104 ---
5 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
80/2026 registered at police station 
Mawana, District Meerut, Uttar Pradesh; 
ii. A direction to forthwith handover the 
mortal remains and ashes of the deceased 
to the petitioner being the mother of the 
deceased;  
iii. A direction for a departmental enquiry into 
the conduct of the investigation officers 
responsible for the initial bungling in 
investigation and cremation of the mortal 
remains and; 
iv. A direction for payment of compensation to 
the petitioner.  
11. The respondents, in their counter affidavit, have 
admitted that pursuant to the recovery of the dead 
body owing to lack of identification, the same was 
kept preserved at the cold storage mortuary of LLRM 
Medical College for a period of 72 hours. When 
exhaustive search efforts from 21 st February to 25 th 
February, 2026 remained unfruitful, and the body 
was neither identified nor claimed by anyone, the 
post mortem was carried out.  Keeping in view the 
articles worn by the deceased namely, a bangle and a 

--- Page 105 ---
6 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
sacred thread on the hand, the investigating agency 
formed a prima facie  opinion that the deceased 
woman followed the Hindu faith. Consequently, the 
mortal remains were cremated at Surajkund  
Crematorium, Meerut as per the prescribed 
procedure. The fact regarding preservation of four 
biological samples viz. right thigh muscle with skin, 
one tooth, a piece of sternum bone and scalp hair is 
also stated in the counter.  
12. As per the reply, CCTV footage from the nearby 
areas was collected and thereafter, four accused 
persons were apprehended who were reportedly 
present in the hotel Avika where the deceased had 
stayed. The CCTV footage also revealed that the dead 
body was taken in a Creta Car and was thrown over 
the boundary wall at about 00:21 hours  on 18 th 
February, 2026.  
13. It is further stated  that, before the dead body 
was cremated , the investigation agency obtained a 
fresh opinion f rom the Medical Board regarding the 
cause of deat h. The reconstituted Medical Board 
opined that death asphyxia due to antemortem 
strangulation could not be ruled out. Upon 
conclusion of the investigation , a charge sheet has 

--- Page 106 ---
7 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
been filed against four accused persons who were 
apprehended by the police during the course of 
investigation.   
14. The State has , of course tried to defend the 
actions of the investigation officers claiming that the 
investigation was conducted with due diligence etc. 
The allegation of the petitioner that the investigation 
was compromised, inadequate, misplaced or tainted 
has been denied. However, insofar as the ashes of the 
deceased are concerned , learned Standing Counsel 
appearing for the State on instructions of the officer 
in charge, candidly conceded that the ashes were not 
preserved and only the viscera articles referred to 
supra have been preserved. Learned Standing 
Counsel also did not seriously contest the prayer of 
the petitioner seeking investigation by a Special 
Investigation Team.  
15. In view of the facts  and circumstances  noted 
above, we are prima facie of the view that the 
allegation levelled in the writ petition that 
investigation conducted by the local police officials  
was shoddy and inadequate is amply supported by 
the material available on record. The delay in 
registration of the FIR, the delay in conducting the 

--- Page 107 ---
8 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
post mortem and the manner in which the opinion 
regarding cause of death was received are all 
indicative of slipshod lackadaisical manner in which 
investigation was conducted. As the dead  body had 
been received with corrosive burns on the face, the 
first attempt of the investigation officer should have 
been to gather the evidence regarding the cause of 
death.  Once there was physical evidence of 
mutilation of the body which was found abandoned 
in a field, there could not have been any reason for 
not registering the FIR promptly. 
16. Be that as it may, the post mortem was deferred 
for almost four days without any justification.  
17. The negligence of the investigation officer is  
further manifested from the fact that the ashes 
pursuant to the cremation of the dead body were 
never preserved, thereby, depriving the petitioner of 
even the satisfaction of taking home the ashes of her 
daughter.   
18. In this view of the matter, we deem it 
appropriate to issue the following directions. 
i. The mortal remains of the deceased 
collected by the doctors during the 
autopsy i.e., right thigh muscle with skin, 

--- Page 108 ---
9 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO(S).313 OF 2026  
 
one tooth, a piece of sternum bone and 
scalp hair shall be handed over to the 
petitioner forthwith under a duly prepared 
memorandum attested by two witnesses.   
These articles shall be handed over to the 
petitioner on Friday (25 th September, 
2026) in the precincts of the Supreme 
Court between 12 PM to 1 PM.  A certified 
copy of the memorandum shall also be 
provided to the petitioner along with the 
mortal remains.  
ii. The Director General of Police, Uttar 
Pradesh shall assign further investigation 
of the matter to a Special Investigation 
Team, headed by an officer not below the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).        OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO(S).16909/2026)
AKSHAY KUMAR VERMA                          …APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH              …RESPONDENT
J U D G M E N T
NAGARATHNA, J.
Issue notice to the respondent.
2. Learned  Government  Advocate  appearing  for  the
respondent-State, who is present in the Court, accepts notice.
3. Leave granted.
4. Briefly stated, the facts of the case as per prosecution are
that Muskan alias, Rinku Verma (since deceased) was married
to the accused-appellant Akshay Kumar Verma (hereinafter
referred to as the “appellant”) on 24.05.2013 and thereafter,
1

--- Page 122 ---
they started residing together with the family of the appellant
in village Sathini.
5. On 26.05.2014, an information regarding death of
Muskan was received by the Station House Officer at
Mangavan Police Station from Ashish Verma, brother-in-law of
the deceased that the deceased had committed suicide by
hanging herself at her matrimonial home. As the said death
had occurred within a few months of marriage, inquest
proceedings were initiated to investigate the circumstances of
her death.
6. During the said inquest proceedings, broken pieces of
bangles of the deceased along with her earrings were
discovered at the spot of occurrence. Further, during the said
inquest proceedings, statements of the father, mother and
other relatives of the deceased were recorded wherein it was
stated that from the inception of the marriage, the deceased's
husband  Akshay  Kumar  Verma,  mother-in-law  Kalawati
Verma, sister-in-law Priyanka, and brother-in-law Ashish
Verma had demanded a motorcycle and Rs.50000/- cash in
2

--- Page 123 ---
dowry. Due to non-fulfillment of the said dowry demands, they
continuously tortured her physically and mentally. Based on
the  aforesaid  information,  FIR  No.247  of  2014  dated
29.05.2014 was registered at Police Station:Mangawan under
Section 498A, 302, 201 read with Section 34 of Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (hereinafter, ‘IPC’) against the appellant herein and
his family members.
7. The Trial Court in Session Trial No.245/2014,  vide
judgment and order dated 16.05.2017, convicted the appellant
under Section 302 of IPC and thereby sentenced him to
undergo rigorous imprisonment for life alongwith fine of
Rs.1000/-. He was further convicted under Section 498A of
IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two
years along with fine of Rs.1000/-.
8. Aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 16.05.2017 of
the Trial Court, the appellant preferred Criminal Appeal
No.2273 of 2017 before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Jabalpur.
9. The High Court, vide impugned judgment and order dated
3

--- Page 124 ---
29.06.2026, dismissed the Criminal Appeal No.2273 of 2017
and thereby affirmed the conviction and sentence of the
appellant under Sections 302 and 498A of IPC.
10. Aggrieved, by the impugned judgment and order dated
29.06.2026, the appellant has preferred the present appeal.
11. Heard learned counsel for the appellant as well as the
learned counsel for the State.
12. Learned counsel for the appellant made a two-fold
submission: firstly, he contended that the High Court was not
right in affirming the judgment of conviction and imposition of
sentence by the Trial Court on merits. Alternatively, learned
counsel for the appellant submitted that in case, this Court is
not inclined to consider the matter on merits, this Court may
remand the matter to the High Court for a re-hearing of the
Criminal Appeal as the High Court has failed to give any
reason whatsoever for confirming the judgment of conviction
and sentence of the Trial Court. 
13. In this regard, learned counsel for the appellant drew our
4

--- Page 125 ---
attention to the impugned judgment and stated that the
judgment consists of only twelve paragraphs, of which, eight
paragraphs record a few facts and contentions and the
consideration of the appeal on merits is only from paragraphs
9 to 10. There being no reason assigned by the High Court for
confirming the judgment of the Trial Court, this Court may set
aside the impugned judgment and remand the matter to the
High Court for rehearing of the appeal and adjudicating the
same in accordance with law.
14. Per  contra ,  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent(s)-State contended that when the High Court, on
hearing the learned counsel for the respective parties, was
inclined to affirm the judgment of conviction and sentence
imposed by the Trial Court, it was unnecessary to give reasons
in detail and therefore, there is no merit in this appeal.
15. During the course of submissions, it was also brought to
our notice that the appellant has completed twelve years’ and
three months of actual sentence and sixteen years’ and seven
months with remission.
5

--- Page 126 ---
16. Learned counsel for the appellant therefore contended
that in case this Court is inclined to remand the matter to the
high court having regard to the long incarceration and the fact
that the appellant has a good case on merits and the matter
now to be reheard by the High Court, the relief of interim bail
may be granted to the appellant herein subject to the
conditions to be imposed on him.
17. We have perused the impugned judgment and we are
inclined to accept the second submission of learned counsel for
the appellant. We find that even if the High Court was
confirming the judgment of conviction and sentence, it ought
to have done so by adequate reasoning on re-appreciation of
the evidence and not in a cryptic manner by which it has
arrived at the conclusion in the impugned judgment. On that
short ground alone, we set aside the impugned judgment and
remand the matter to the High Court.
18. The High Court is requested to rehear the appeal, re-
appreciate the entire evidence on record and adjudicate the
same in accordance with law.
6

--- Page 127 ---
19. Since the appellant has been in jail for the last sixteen
years’ and seven months with remission and twelve years’ and
three months without remission, we find that pending
consideration of the appeal by the High Court, the ends of
justice would be met if we grant the relief(s) of suspension of
sentence and interim bail to the appellant herein. 
20. We, therefore, allow this appeal by setting aside the
impugned judgment and remanding the matter to the High
Court and direct as under:
“The appellant shall be produced before the concerned
Trial Court as early as possible and the Trial Court shall
release him on bail, subject to such conditions as it may deem
appropriate  to  impose  to  ensure  his  presence  in  the
proceedings.”
21. The appellant shall appear before the High Court as and
when directed to do so. 
22. It is directed that the appellant shall extend complete
cooperation in the hearing of the appeal before the High Court.
7

--- Page 128 ---
23. The appellant shall not misuse his liberty in any manner.
 
24. Any infraction of the conditions may entail cancellation of
the suspension of sentence and interim bail granted to the
appellant. 
25. With these observations, the criminal appeal is allowed.
.………………………………………, J.
(B.V. NAGARATHNA)
………………………………………, J.

I.A. No. 279214/2026:
Heard Ms. Kavitha Rameshwar Nithyanandam, learned AAG
appearing for the State of Tamil Nadu/applicants, namely,
the Chief Secretary and the Director General of Police,
Tamil Nadu.
5

--- Page 136 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO. 11263/2025
2. Learned AAG submits that the present application has
been filed seeking recall of the order dated 05.08.2026
passed by this Court, specifically the direction contained
in paragraph 9 thereof, whereby notice of Contempt was
directed to be issued to the Chief Secretary and the
Director General of Police, Tamil Nadu, for not having
filed their affidavits despite the earlier directions of
this Court. It is submitted that the requisite affidavit
had in fact been filed on 04.08.2026, but inadvertently
the same was not reflected in the Office Report. It is
further submitted that the Registry of this Court pursuant
to the aforesaid direction, issued the notice of Contempt
against the applicants, which is sought to be recalled. 
3. Mr. S.D. Sanjay, learned Senior Advocate/Coordinator
and  Convenor  in  the  present  case,  admits  that  the
affidavit on behalf of the State of Tamil Nadu had been
served on him on 30.07.2026 itself.
4. Having regard to the aforesaid, the prayer made in the
application is allowed. The notice of Contempt issued
against the Chief Secretary and the Director General of
Police,  State  of  Tamil  Nadu,  stands  withdrawn.  Their
personal  appearance  also  stands  dispensed  with.
Consequently,  the  Interlocutory  Application  stands
disposed of.
6

--- Page 137 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO. 11263/2025
I.A. No.284693/2026:

of  Punjab  seeking  modification  of  the  order  dated
05.08.2026, by which notice of Contempt was issued against
the Chief Secretary and the Director General of Police,
Punjab. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State
of Punjab submits that the affidavit had been filed on

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                                O R D E R
1. Petitioner  is  in  jail  since
16.03.2022  for  having  allegedly  committed
offence  punishable  under  Sections
406/420/467/468/471/120-B  of  Indian  Penal
Code, 1860 in connection with EOW-CID, CB PS
Case No. 17/2021 corresponding to CT Case No.
35/2023, which is now pending trial before
the competent Court.
2. Learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State of Odisha would object to
the petitioner’s prayer for grant of bail on
the submission that the offence committed by
the  petitioner  involves  cheating  and
misappropriation by a finance company namely,
Sambandh Finserve Pvt. Ltd, (SFPL), which is
a Non-Banking Financial Company-Micro Finance
Institution  (NBFC-MFI)  approved  and
registered  with  Reserve  Bank  of  India  as
Micro Finance Institution (MFI) and since,
the amount involved is huge, considering the
gravity  of  offence,  petitioner  is  not
entitled to be released on bail.
3. It  is  also  submitted  that  the
petitioner has 06 more criminal antecedents

3

PC Act 1988 and under Sections 120-B, 420,
409,468 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 by the Central Bureau of Investigation
(CBI).
4. It is brought to our notice that
petitioner has already been released in five
other offence of similar nature registered
with different Police Stations.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 12034 of 2026)
UTKARSH KASHYAP APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN     RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 12100 of 2026)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant  before  this  Court  has  filed  the
present appeals, being aggrieved by the impugned common
order  dated  27.04.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature for Rajasthan Bench at Jaipur in S.B. Criminal
Miscellaneous Bail Application Nos. 1914 and 2624 of 2026,
rejecting the prayer for bail in connection with FIR No.
373 of 2025, registered at Police Station Sodala, Jaipur
City (East), for the offences punishable under Sections
318(4), 316(2) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (for short ‘BNS’) and FIR No. 762 of 2025, registered
1

--- Page 200 ---
at Police Station Pratap Nagar, Jaipur City (East), for the
offences punishable under Sections 318(4) and 316(2) of the
BNS. 
3. As per the prosecution case, the appellant along
with other persons lured the complainant with promises of
huge profits, and an agreement was executed between the
parties on 08.07.2024. It was promised that the complainant
would be granted a franchise of Taskar Global Private
Limited.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant has argued that at
the relevant point of time, the appellant was merely an
employee of the company and no action has been taken
against the Directors involved in the matter, who have not
been arrested so far. It is further stated that the
signatories to the agreement, namely, Pawan Kumar Sharma
and Raghuveer Singh, have already been granted bail vide
orders dated 29.01.2026 and 04.08.2026 respectively. The
aforesaid factual position has not been disputed by learned
counsel for the respondent-State.
5. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  has
vehemently opposed the prayer for grant of bail, contending
that  there  is  suppression  of  material  facts  as  the
appellant  has  not  disclosed  his  complete  criminal
antecedents. It is further submitted that the appellant is
2

--- Page 201 ---
presently a Director of the company. However, it is stated
that he became a Director subsequent to 03.10.2025, which
is the date on which the FIR was lodged. There is no
document on record establishing that the appellant became a
Director prior to the lodging of the FIR.
6. Keeping in view of the fact that two other co-
accused persons have already been granted bail and that the
alleged  offences  are  triable  by  a  Magistrate,  the
application for grant of bail deserves to be allowed and is
accordingly allowed.
7. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.
8. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial
court and subject to such other terms and conditions as may
be imposed by it.
9. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
10. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
11. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall
3

--- Page 202 ---
diligently  attend  proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending the
proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also be
seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the
trial court will be free to pass appropriate orders.
12. We clarify that the observations made in this order
and grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the
merits of the case.
13. The  appeals  are,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the
aforesaid terms.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The above appeal arises from an order of interim
maintenance  passed  by  the  Metropolitan  Magistrate,
Karkardooma Courts, affirmed by the Additional Sessions
Judge and subsequently by Single Judge Bench of the High
Court of Delhi. Before us, when the matter was posted, we
directed the parties to be present, especially since we
were not inclined to interfere with the order passed.
3. The appellant and the respondent got married in the
year 2010 and there is a child born in the wedlock, who is
16 years old. The appellant, in the course of hearing,
submitted that he is willing to pay Rs.30,00,000/- as
2

--- Page 219 ---
SLP(Crl.) No.17762/2026
interim maintenance to settle the entire disputes and also
obtain a decree of divorce on the ground of irretrievable
breakdown of marriage, provided he is at least given two
years’ time to make the deposit. The wife consented readily
and we directed them to reduce the terms of settlement into
writing with a clear schedule of payment and file it before
us.
4. Today when the matter was taken up, the Settlement
Agreement between the parties dated 22.09.2026, was placed
on record. The schedule of payment, as agreed between the
parties, is as hereunder:
Installment
No(s)
Due date Amount
1 05.10.2026 Rs.6,00,000/-
2 15.03.2027 Rs.6,00,000/-
3 15.09.2027 Rs.6,00,000/-
4 15.03.2028 Rs.6,00,000/-
5 15.09.2028 Rs.6,00,000/-
Total: Rs.30,00,000/-
(Rupees  Thirty  Lakhs
Only)
5. Learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the
appellant desires that the money would only be used for the
3

--- Page 220 ---
SLP(Crl.) No.17762/2026
purpose of education of the son and the wife readily agreed
to it. However, we are not inclined to pass any such order
since the mother having custody, will have to decide on how
to use the money paid by the appellant as alimony, which is
primarily for maintenance of the wife and also in the best
interest of the child. We would think that the mother
having custody of the child would be the best person to
decide on the manner in which the money is to be used. In
that circumstance, we also modify the settlement agreed
upon by the parties as to the transfer of money. 
6. We  are  of  the  opinion  that  the  money  should  be
transferred into the account of the mother itself. Learned
Counsel for the respondent shall supply the details of the
mother’s  account  to  the  appellant’s  Counsel  and  the
appellant shall pay the amounts in accordance with the
settlement to that account.
7. Considering the fact that the payment schedule runs
over two years, we are of the opinion that if one default
is committed, the respondent-wife should be given liberty
4

--- Page 221 ---
SLP(Crl.) No.17762/2026
to move this Court to proceed appropriately against the
appellant-husband.
8. The  terms  of  the  settlement  are  not  extracted
hereunder since the matter has not been finalized as of
now. The settlement will be kept on record and it will be
taken up when the entire amount is paid to the account of
the respondent-wife, for consideration of the prayer for
dissolution of marriage on irretrievable grounds, invoking
our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.
9. In  the  meanwhile,  it  is  made  clear  that  the
proceedings between the parties, both criminal and civil,

    O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Bench at Indore, by
the impugned judgment and order dated 27th February, 2026,
has rejected the appellant’s application for grant of bail.
3. Appellant, figuring as an accused in FIR No.0422 of
2025 dated 02nd September, 2025 registered at Police Station
Khudel, District Indore Rural, Madhya Pradesh under Sections
420, 467, 468, 471, 120-B and 34 of  the Indian Penal Code,
1860, was arrested on 07th November, 2025.
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.9741/2026 1

--- Page 224 ---
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the counter-affidavit of the respondent-State of
Madhya Pradesh.
5. The prosecution proposes to examine 18 witnesses.
6. It appears that charges are yet to be framed against
the appellant despite charge-sheet having been filed on 10 th
February, 2026.
7. The disclosure statement has led to recovery of the
original General Power of Attorney.
8. Taking an overall view of the matter, coupled with the
period of incarceration of the appellant and the likely time to
be taken to complete the trial, we are of the considered
opinion  that  further  detention  of  the appellant is  not
necessary; and, since the appeal deserve acceptance, the
appellant may be admitted to an order for grant of bail
pending trial.
9. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and
order.
10. Appellant  shall  be  released  on  bail,  subject  to
Crl. Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No.9741/2026 2

--- Page 225 ---
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court
and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be
imposed by it.
11. Needless to observe, if released on bail, the appellant
shall not, directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
12. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty
to cancel the bail of the appellant.
13. It is also ordered that the appellant shall diligently
attend proceedings of the trial, unless exempted. If he
abstains from attending the proceedings without justifiable
cause, that could also be seen as breach of the conditions for
grant of bail and the trial court will be free to pass
appropriate orders.
14. We clarify that the observations made in this order and
grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of
the case.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13105 OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO.33281/2025)
MELVIN BENNYACHAN                                  APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE COMPANY LTD.                RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Heard  Mr.  Sugam  Agrawal,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner and Mr. Amit Kumar Singh, learned counsel for the
respondent-Insurance Company.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  quantum  of
compensation awarded by the High Court, though the same has
been enhanced as compared to the Motor Accident Claims
Tribunal,  Muvattupuzha,  which  had  awarded  Rs.14,85,985/-
(Rupees Fourteen Lakhs Eighty Five Thousand Nine Hundred and
Eighty Five) with 9% interest per annum, whereas the High
Court has enhanced it to Rs.29,72,770/- (Rupees Twenty Nine
Lakhs Seventy Two Thousand Seven Hundred and Seventy) while
reducing the interest to 8% per annum.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that on
1

--- Page 236 ---
account  of  the  accident,  the  appellant  had  to  undergo
amputation of his right leg below knee and thus, he was
permanently disabled from carrying out his profession as he
was an Electrician. It was further submitted that for leading
a normal life, he has to use a prosthetic limb, which is
expensive and a reasonable estimation of the cost which may
be  incurred  is  Rs.2,50,000/-  (Rupees  Two  Lakhs  Fifty
Thousand) for the prosthetic limb and at least Rs.15,000/-
(Rupees Fifteen Thousand) per annum for its maintenance. It
was submitted that in a similar situation, a Coordinate Bench
of this Court in Civil Appeal No.4642 of 2026, titled
“Prahlad  Sahai  vs.  Haryana  Roadways  and  Another”  vide
judgment dated 21.04.2026, where the victim had suffered
amputation and was 32 years of age, had awarded the cost of
prosthetic @ Rs.2,50,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs Fifty Thousand)
per prosthetic limb every five years till the age of 70 years
and additional maintenance of Rs.15,000/- (Rupees Fifteen
Thousand) per annum.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent-Insurance Company
submitted  that  the  amount  of  compensation  is  quite
reasonable. However, he could not contest with regard to the
amount which the Coordinate Bench had awarded under similar
circumstances,  specifically  with  regard  to  the  cost  of
prosthetic limb and maintenance thereof.
6. Having considered the matter, we find no reason to take
a different view from the one taken by the Coordinate Bench
2

--- Page 237 ---
in the case of Prahlad Sahai (supra).
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed by quantifying and
awarding a further compensation of Rs.25,00,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Five Lakhs) lump sum, which would be in addition to
the compensation awarded by the High Court under the order
impugned. The same be paid to the appellant after adjusting
the amount already paid, within eight weeks from today. We
clarify that the lump sum amount of Rs.25,00,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Five Lakhs) awarded under this order shall not carry
any interest.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
.....................J.
(AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)

O R D E R
    1.   Leave granted.
2.  The appellant before this Court has filed the
present  appeal  being  aggrieved  by  order  dated
02.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Calcutta in CRM
(NDPS) No.1263 of 2025, rejecting the prayer for bail
of  the  appellant  in  connection  with  NDPS  Case
No.260/2025 pending before the Special Judge, 8 th Court
at Barasat, North 24 Parganas.
3. The allegation against the appellant is that the
appellant was carrying 5990 grams of ganja along with
the co-accused, who were carrying 5.990 kg of ganja,
making a total quantity of 11.975 kilograms of ganja.
They were apprehended by the Air Customs Department at
Kolkata Airport and taken into custody.
4.  Learned counsel for the appellant has argued
before this Court that the co-accused has already been
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  7446/2026  ]

--- Page 251 ---
2
granted bail by the High Court. The aforesaid fact has
not been disputed by the learned counsel for the
respondent. It has also been stated that the appellant
is in jail for the last one year. 
5. This Court, after hearing the learned counsel for
the parties and keeping in view the quantity of Ganja
recovered  from  the  appellant,  the  period  of
incarceration already undergone by him, and the fact
that the other co-accused has already been enlarged on
bail, is of the opinion that the appellant has made out
a case for interference with the impugned order dated
02.02.2026.  This  Court  is  of  the  view  that  the
appellant's further detention is not necessary pending
trial. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed, and the
appellant is directed to be released on bail, subject
to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the
learned Trial Court.
6. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts
of the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
7. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be
at liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Petitioner has been convicted under Section 302
1

--- Page 256 ---
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) by
the Additional Sessions Judge, Titilagarh, Odisha in
Sessions Case No.15 of 2011 and sentenced to undergo
Rigorous Imprisonment for Life and to pay Rs.25,000/-
as fine with a default stipulation.
3. Appeal  filed  by  the  petitioner  against  his
conviction and sentence was rejected by the High
Court of Odisha at Cuttack (briefly the ‘High Court’
hereinafter),  vide  the  judgment  and  order  dated
27.10.2021.
4. On the basis of custody certificate, it can be
seen that as of now, petitioner has been in jail for
almost 15 years 07 months.
5. On  15.06.2026,  we  had  issued  notice  on  the
Special Leave Petition as well as on the prayer for
suspension of sentence.
6. This Court, in the case of In Re: Policy Strategy
for Grant of Bail [2025 SCC OnLine SC 349],  recorded
the following conclusions:
“21.  We,  therefore,  record  the  following
conclusions:
a) Where  there  is  a  policy  of  the
appropriate Government laying down guidelines
for consideration of the grant of premature
release under Section 432 of the CrPC or
Section 473 of the BNSS, it is the obligation
of the appropriate Government to consider
cases of all convicts for grant of premature
release as and when they become eligible for
consideration in terms of the policy. In such
2

--- Page 257 ---
a case, it is not necessary for the convict
or  his  relatives  to  make  a  specific
application for grant of permanent remission.
When  the  jail  manual  or  any  other
departmental  instruction  issued  by  the
appropriate Government contains such policy
guidelines,  the  aforesaid  direction  will
apply;
b) We  direct  those  States  and  Union
Territories that do not have a policy dealing
with the grant of remission in terms of
Section 432 of the CrPC or Section 473 of the
BNSS to formulate a policy within two months
from today;
c) Appropriate Government has the power to
incorporate suitable conditions in an order
granting permanent remission. Consideration
of various factors, which are mentioned in
paragraph 13 above by way of illustration, is
necessary before finalizing the conditions.
The conditions must aim at ensuring that the
criminal tendencies, if any, of the convict
remain  in  check  and  that  the  convict
rehabilitates himself in the society. The
conditions should not be so oppressive or
stringent that the convict is not able to
take  advantage  of  the  order  granting
permanent remission. The conditions cannot be
vague  and  should  be  capable  of  being
performed;
d) Order granting or refusing the relief of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons. The order containing reasons should
be immediately communicated to the convict
through the office of the concerned prison.
The copies thereof should be forwarded to the
Secretaries of the concerned District Legal
Services Authorities. It is the duty of the
prison authorities to inform the convict that
3

--- Page 258 ---
he has the right to challenge the order of
rejection of the prayer for the grant of
remission.
e) As held in the case of Mafabhai Motibhai
Sagar, an order granting permanent remission
cannot  be  withdrawn  or  cancelled  without
giving an opportunity of being heard to the
convict.  An  order  of  cancellation  of
permanent  remission  must  contain  brief
reasons;
f) The District Legal Services Authorities
shall endeavour to implement NALSA SOP in its
true letter and spirit.
g) Further,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall also monitor implementation
of conclusion (a) as recorded above. For this
purpose,  the  District  Legal  Services
Authorities shall maintain the relevant date
of the convicts and as and when they become
eligible to a consideration for grant of
premature release, they shall do the needful
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal
Services  Authorities  shall  endeavour  to
create  a  portal  on  which  the  data  as
aforesaid  can  be  uploaded  on  real  time
basis.”
7. In terms of Paragraph 21(g) of the conclusions
extracted  herein  above,  District  Legal  Services
Authorities  have  been  mandated  to  monitor
implementation of conclusion (a). For this purpose,
the  District  Legal  Services  Authorities  shall
maintain the relevant data of the convicts and as and
when they become eligible for a consideration for
grant of premature release, they shall do the needful
4

--- Page 259 ---
in terms of conclusion (a). The State Legal Services
Authorities shall endeavour to create a portal on
which the data as aforesaid can be uploaded on real
time basis.
8. We, therefore, direct the appropriate Government,
i.e. State of Odisha, to consider the case for
permanent remission of the petitioner as per the
applicable remission policy.
9. The  District  Legal  Services  Authority  of
Titilagarh shall do the needful so that the remission
papers of the petitioner can be transmitted to the
State Government for necessary consideration.
10. In  view  of  the  long  incarceration  of  the
petitioner, we direct, as an interim measure, that
the petitioner shall be released on bail from custody
on his Personal Bond.
11. Interim bail granted to the petitioner shall not
be taken as a factor against the petitioner while
considering his case for permanent remission.
12. Let the consideration be carried out within 03
months from today.
13. List thereafter on 20.01.2027.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.9810/2026)
KANHA @ KANHAIYA SINGH      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
3. Appellant(s) is aggrieved by order dated 20.03.2026
passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Indore
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.548/2025
registered at Police Station- Station Road, District-
Ratlam, Madhya Pradesh under Sections 137(2), 65(2), 64(2)
(m) and 87 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short, ‘BNS’); Sections 3(A), 4(2) and 5(m)/6 of the
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for
short, ‘POCSO Act’); and Sections 3(1)(w)(II) and 3(2)(v)
of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention
1

--- Page 261 ---
of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
5. The accusation against the appellant is that he was a
tenant  residing  in  the  neighbourhood  of  the  victim.
Despite being a married person, he attempted to abduct the
elder sister of the victim leading to registration of
Crime No.259/2025. Thereafter, the victim informed her
mother that appellant had sexually exploited her for about
a month, leading to registration of the present case.
6. Appellant is in custody since 10.09.2025.
7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
24.07.2026, pursuant to which respondent-State of Madhya
Pradesh has filed counter affidavit to which appellant has
filed rejoinder affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
present case is a fallout of his relationship with the
elder sister of the so called victim. It is only to harass
the appellant for his involvement with the elder daughter
that the present case has been registered. In any view of
the matter, appellant has been in custody for more than
one year now. Therefore, appellant should be enlarged on
bail.
9. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Madhya
Pradesh, on the other hand, submits that appellant has
been  convicted  in  the  case  arising  out  of  Crime
NO.259/2025  on  01.07.2026.  In  the  present  case,
prosecutrix is a minor girl and the accusation against the
appellant is serious. Insofar the trial is concerned,
2

--- Page 262 ---
prosecution proposes to examine 15 witnesses, out of which
05 witnesses have been examined. In such circumstances,
releasing the appellant on bail may not be appropriate.
10. Responding to the above, learned counsel for the
appellant submits that appellant has preferred an appeal
against his conviction and is confident of success in the
appeal. Insofar the present case is concerned, he submits
that he has been falsely implicated in this case only with
a view to teach him a lesson.
11. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the materials on record.
12. From a perusal of the impugned order, we find that
the High Court declined to grant bail to the appellant,
taking  the  view  that  granting  of  bail  may  have
ramifications on the social order and the “morals” of the
victim’s family.
13. We are of the view that Courts should refrain from
imposing the personal views or value judgment of the
Presiding  Judge  on  morality  or  otherwise  while
adjudicating a matter relating to bail, or even a criminal
trial of an accused.
14. Insofar the present case is concerned, we find that
appellant has already undergone more than one year of
incarceration. It would take some more time for the trial
to conclude. In such circumstances, we are of the view
that a case for bail is made out.
15. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
3

--- Page 263 ---
20.03.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
16. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the concerned jurisdictional Special Court
within a maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter
he shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate. This bail order would be
subject to the appellant being in custody in the connected
criminal appeal where he has assailed his conviction by
the Trial Court.
17. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

      UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard  Mr. Nikhil Goel,  learned Senior Counsel for
the  petitioner  and  Ms.  Swati  Ghildiyal,, learned
counsel for the State.
2. The  present  petition  calls  in  question  the
correctness  of  the  order  dated  08-05-2026  in
R/CRLMA(For  Regular  Bail-After  Chargesheet)
No.26773/2025 passed by the High Court of Gujarat at
Ahmedabad. By the said order, the petitioner has been
denied the benefit of bail in connection with FIR being
C.R.No.11210047250893/2025 registered with Udhna/Udhana
Police Station, Surat City, Gujarat, for the offences
punishable under Sections 318(4), 336(2), 338, 336(3),
340(2), 61(2) & 3(5) of  the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023  and  under  Section  66D  of  the  Information
Technology Act, 2000.
3. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner contends
that the petitioner has already undergone about one
year and two months in custody; that the offences are
Magistrate triable; that the prosecution has listed 122
witnesses; that out of the 30 accused persons set up
for the trial, four accused persons, namely, Mayurbhai,
Dipakbhai, Kalpeshbhai and Arunbhai, who are on bail
have broadly similar case to that of the petitioner
herein; that the chargesheet and other documents run

--- Page 285 ---
3
into one and a half lakh pages, and that the trial is
bound to take considerable amount of time to conclude.
4. Learned counsel for the State vehemently opposes the
bail prayer of the petitioner, submits that it is a
case where the petitioner was a Area Head of all the
branches  of  RBL  Bank,  situated  in  Surat,  has
facilitated the opening of mule accounts and for every
account on a running basis charged 0.20% as commission
alone according to the learned counsel for the State
amounts to Rs.1.1 crore.
5. We  have  considered  the  rival  submissions;
considering  the  period  already  undergone  by  the
petitioner;  the  fact  that  offences  are  Magistrate
triable; the fact that four other accused persons
having broadly a similar role have been granted bail
and keeping in mind the time that the trial will take
to conclude, we are inclined to enlarge the petitioner
on bail.
6. Accordingly, we direct that petitioner shall be
enlarged on bail subject to the satisfaction of the
concerned Trial Court in connection with the aforesaid
FIR/C.R.  case  and  for  the  offences  mentioned
hereinabove.
7. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant challenges the judgment and order dated
06-01-2025 in SBCRP No. 283/2024 titled “ Ashok  Kumar  Ahuja
vs.  Pandit  Shrikant  &  Ors .” passed by the High Court of
Judicature for Rajasthan at Jaipur.
3. As prayed for, names of respondent nos. 2,3,5 & 6 stand
deleted subject to just exceptions.
4. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we are of
the considered view that the impugned judgment and order
deserves to be quashed and set aside, for we do not find the
application of respondent no.1, filed under Order VII Rule 11
CPC to contain any particulars warranting a favourable order.
The application ought to have disclosed material particulars
1

--- Page 292 ---
which are conspicuously silent and does not even remotely
meet the statutory requirements seeking rejection of the
plaint at the threshold on the specified grounds.
5. We notice that the Trial Court had, in fact, rejected
the application by assigning cogent reasons.  However, the
High Court for reasons not emanating from the record, allowed
the  same  which  approach  adopted  by  the  High  Court  is
extremely fallacious.  Hence, the impugned judgment and order
passed by the High Court, is quashed and set aside and Civil
Suit No.34/2022 is restored to its original number and
position.
6. Since the suit was instituted in the year 2022, we
direct  the  parties  to  fully  co-operate;  not  take  any
unnecessary adjournment(s); defendants to file their written
statement within eight weeks; pleadings be completed within
four weeks thereafter and the trial be expedited.
7. The parties shall appear before the Trial Court on 19 th
August, 2026.
8. With the above observations, appeal stands disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.7369/2011
YENKANGOUDA & ANR.                              APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
AMBAMMA (DEAD) BY LR. & ORS.                   RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7463/2011
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellants and the learned counsel appearing for the
respondents.
2. The suit has been filed by the respondents for partition
on the premise that the respondent/plaintiff is the
legally  wedded  wife  of  the  paternal  uncle  of  the
defendant No.1. Four witnesses have been examined on

--- Page 304 ---
2
behalf  of  the  respondents/plaintiffs.  Additionally,
documentary evidence in the form of Voters list and
Aadhar Card have also been marked. The Trial Court, upon
framing the issue as to whether the plaintiff/respondent
No.1 is the legally wedded wife of the paternal uncle of
defendant no.1, has held in the affirmative and granted
the plaintiffs a ½ share. Initially, the Regular First
Appeal filed before the High Court was dismissed and the
decree of the Trial Court was confirmed. 
3. However, the judgment of the High Court has been set
aside by the Supreme Court on the earlier occasion and
the matter was remanded to the High Court for fresh
consideration. Subsequently, the appeal remitted to High
Court was partly allowed by modifying the share granted
by the Trial Court from ½ to 1/7th share. 
4. Though,  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellants/defendants  submitted  that  there  is  no
documentary evidence available, the fact remains that
apart from the oral evidence which was duly considered by
both  the  Courts,  there  were  documentary  evidences
available in the form of Aadhar Card and Voters List
indicating that plaintiff No. 1 was the wife of the
deceased – Somappa, who is the paternal uncle of the
present appellants/defendants.

--- Page 305 ---
3
5. In such view of the matter, we do not find any perversity
with the impugned order warranting any interference in
the present appeals.
6. The appeals stand dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 367/2026
MAJOR KSHITIJ MAAN & ANR. ..... PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
POONAM ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We find from the cause title of this transfer petition that
the petitioners indicated the details of the respondent-wife
as under: -
“Poonam
Aged about 33 years,
D/o Sh. Krishna Kumar, Resident of House NO. 56,
Village Shyam Kalyan, District Charkhi Dadri, Haryana
– 127306.
Email: poonamragi308@gamil.com
Mobile No.: +91-807696024”
2. We may note that the mobile number of the respondent shown in
the cause title was incomplete, as one digit was completely
left out and the mobile number, as set out, had only nine
digits.  Further, we are informed by the respondent-wife, who
appears as a party-in-person, that the pin code shown for her
ancestral address is also incorrect, as it is 127306 and not
127030.  That apart, even the email address is also shown
1

--- Page 316 ---
incorrectly as “gamil.com” and not “gmail.com”.
3. More significantly, the respondent, Poonam, pointed out that
she had brought it to the notice of her husband/petitioner No.
1, Major Kshitij Maan, that she was residing at G-1014, Tenth
Floor, Pocket-5, Block-G, Sector-14, Dwarka, New Delhi –
110078, but despite being aware of the same, the petitioners
did not choose to indicate the said address in the cause title
of the transfer petition.
4. In this regard, we may note that the petitioners filed reply
dated 15.09.2026, wherein they admitted that the respondent
had shown her aforestated address at Dwarka, New Delhi, in her
pleadings with effect from 25.07.2025 but had adopted, for the
purpose of service of notice, her ancestral address only.
5. This admission of the petitioners clearly shows that an
attempt was made by them to avoid effecting service  of notice
upon the respondent for obvious reasons. We may also note from
the orders passed in this case on various dates that service
remained incomplete and when the matter was listed before the
Hon’ble Chamber Judge on 20.07.2026, the learned counsel for
the  petitioners  prayed  for  issuance  of  fresh  notice,
submitting that the respondent stays at the given address. The
given address was the ancestral address of the respondent and
the petitioners were well aware, going by their reply dated
15.09.2026, that the respondent was residing at a different
address in Dwarka, New Delhi. The insistence upon issuance of
fresh notice to the same address speaks for itself.
2

--- Page 317 ---
6. The aforestated facts demonstrate clear abuse of process by
the petitioners, rendering this transfer petition liable to be
rejected on that short ground.  The transfer petition is,
accordingly, dismissed.
7. Interim order dated 25.03.2026 shall stand vacated.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

(SANJAY KUMAR)
.........................J.
(SANJEEV SACHDEVA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.13848/2026)
MILU SINKU      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF ODISHA     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. V. N. Raghupathy, learned counsel
for the appellant and Ms. Divya Roy, learned counsel for
the respondent-State of Odisha.
3. On 27.07.2026, we had passed the following order:
“2. The High Court declined to entertain the
Criminal Appeal of the petitioner assailing his
conviction under Section 302 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) on the
ground of inordinate delay. Petitioner is in
custody for more than 12 years now. For delay
of 2538 days in filing the Criminal Appeal, the
High Court dismissed the same.
3. Prima facie, we are of the view that when
the convict is in jail and this being a jail
appeal,  the  same  ought  not  to  have  been
dismissed on the ground of delay and should
have  been  heard  on  merits.  In  such
circumstances ordinarily we would have remanded
1

--- Page 320 ---
the matter to the High Court for hearing on
merits. However, having regard to the fact that
petitioner has already undergone incarceration
of more than 12 years, we do not propose to
remand the matter back to the High Court.
4.  The  delay  in  filing  the  Special  Leave
Petition is condoned.
5. Issue notice, both on the Special Leave
Petition as well as on the prayer for bail,
returnable on 03.09.2026.
6. Permission is accorded to learned counsel
for the petitioner to serve notice upon the
Standing counsel for the respondent-State of
Odisha.”
4. We find that appellant’s appeal before the High Court
of  Orissa  at  Cuttack  (briefly  ‘the  High  Court’
hereinafter), assailing his conviction under Section 302
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’), was not
adjudicated on merit. The same was dismissed on the ground
of belated filing of the appeal.
5. We had already observed in an earlier proceeding that
when it is a statutory appeal by a convict serving jail
sentence, the jail appeal should be heard by the High
Court on merit and should not be dismissed on the ground
of delay. Such an approach goes against the principle of
access to justice, rather the very concept of justice
itself.
6. Considering the above, we set aside the impugned
order dated 05.04.2023 passed by the High Court and
condone the delay in filing the Criminal Appeal before the
2

--- Page 321 ---
High Court.
7. Having  regard  to  the  long  incarceration  of  the
appellant which is more than 12 years now, we grant bail
to the appellant on usual terms and conditions.
8. The matter is remanded back to the High Court for
adjudication of the Criminal Appeal preferred by the
appellant on its own merit.
9. We  request  the  High  Court  to  hear  the  same
expeditiously. We make it clear that appellant shall co-
operate with the Criminal Appeal, now to be heard by the
High Court on its own merit.
10. The Criminal Appeal is, accordingly, disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
…………………………………………………...J.

…………………………………………………...J.
     [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;
23rd SEPTEMBER, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.               /2026  
[Arising out of SLP(C) No. 8751/2026]
MARKANDEY YADAV              APPELLANT
VERSUS
NARESH SHARAMA RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. A  contempt  petition 1 filed  by  the  appellant  has  been
dismissed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad 2 vide an
order dated 02 nd January, 2024 as time-barred. Appellant has
taken exception to such order by filing this appeal.
3. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
4. It appears that a writ petition 3 filed by the appellant was
disposed of with certain directions on 8 th May, 2014. The order
was  not  complied  with  by  the  Director  of  Education
(Madhyamic). Appellant invoked the contempt jurisdiction of the
High Court by filing a petition 4. It was disposed of on 11 th May,
2015  by  directing  the  Director  of  Education  (Madhyamic)  to
decide the claim of the appellant within two weeks. There being
1  Contempt Application Civil No.2413 of 2016
2  High Court
3  Writ C. No.14242 of 2013
4  Contempt Application Civil No.2797 of 2015
1

--- Page 336 ---
no compliance, the appellant was compelled to once again file
for  contempt  which  has  proved  abortive  by  reason  of  the
impugned order. 
5. The High Court relied on the decision of this Court in Pallav
Sheth v. Custodian 5 [3-J], which overruled an earlier decision
in  Om  Prakash  Jaiswal  v.  D.K.  Mittal6 [2-J]. It was held in
Pallav Sheth (supra) that irrespective of the date of initiation of
proceedings for contempt, if a petition alleging contempt is filed
within a year from the date contempt is alleged, it would not be
time barred.  
6. Here, as noticed above, the facts are a bit different. It is not
in dispute that the contempt petition, which has been dismissed
by the impugned order, is the second in the series. The first
petition was filed within a year of contempt having occurred.
The Director of Education (Madhyamic), despite the orders dated
8th May, 2014 and 11 th May, 2015, failed to decide the claim of
the appellant. There being a continuing act of contempt, the
appellant was entitled to exemption from the laws of limitation.
Although no application to that effect was filed, on facts and in
the  circumstances,  we  grant  such  exemption  and  hold  the
second contempt petition to be maintainable.
7. Accordingly, the impugned order is set aside with the result
that Contempt Application (Civil) No.2413/2016 shall revive on
the file of the High Court. The same may now be decided in
5  (2001) 7 SCC 549
6  (2000) 3 SCC 171
2

--- Page 337 ---
accordance with law.
8. The  alleged contemnor  has  reportedly  retired.  We, thus,
grant liberty to the appellant to implead the present incumbent
on the post of Director of Education (Madhyamic) in his place
and stead.
9. At the same time, since it has been submitted by learned
counsel appearing for the respondent that the order has already
been complied with, such fact may be brought to the notice of
the High Court for its due consideration.
10. The appeal stands disposed of on the above terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
...........................................J.
(DIPANKAR DATTA)
.............................................J.
(SHEEL NAGU)
New Delhi;
September 21, 2026.

Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that the  co-accused-Dinesh Kumar is on bail.
According to the learned counsel, Dinesh Kumar was also,
according to the prosecution, present in the vehicle and
according to the Investigating Agency, he fled the scene.
Learned counsel further submits that the petitioner is in
custody for 2 years and 4 months and that only 6, out of
19 witnesses have been examined so far.  The trial is
likely to take long time to conclude.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent-State vehemently
opposes the prayer of the petitioner for bail and submits
that as far as the co-accused-Dinesh Kumar is concerned,
there was no conscious possession.
          SLP (Criminal) No.15848/2026                                                              Page 2 of 3

--- Page 376 ---
5. In response, learned counsel for the petitioner
submits that even according to the prosecution, it was
the co-accused-Dinesh Kumar who was the other passenger
in the vehicle.  In any event, these are the matters for
trial.
6. Considering the overall facts and circumstances;
the fact that the petitioner has undergone 2 years and 4
months in custody; the co-accused-Dinesh Kumar is already
on bail; the trial is likely to take some time to
conclude and keeping in mind the principles enshrined in
Article 21 of the Constitution of India coupled with the
twin conditions of Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and
Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 , we are inclined to
enlarge the petitioner on bail, pending trial.
7. We direct that the petitioner shall be enlarged on
bail subject to the satisfaction of the Trial Court,
pending trial.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
9. Pending applications shall also stand disposed of.

offences punishable under Sections 406 and 420 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 in the Court of J.M. 1 st Class-Cum-
CJJD-XI, Patna, Bihar.
3. At the outset, learned counsel for the petitioners
submits  that,  in  fact,  under  some  misconception  the
petitioners  had  moved  for  anticipatory  bail  in  the
complaint case, when clearly the law has been settled by
this court in the case of  Om  Prakash  Chhawnika  @  Om
Prakash  Chabnika  @  Om  Prakash  Chawnika  vs.  State  of
Jharkhand and Another  [SLP (Crl.) No. 16221 of 2025 dated
23.04.2026], especially paragraph ‘10’ thereof, where it
has been stipulated that the police has no jurisdiction to
arrest a person in a complaint case without there being a
non-bailable warrant issued by the Court concerned along
with the summons.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that in
2

Prakash  Chhawnika  (supra) would squarely apply in the

fairly submits that such position has been settled in the
case of Om Prakash Chhawnika (supra).
6. Having  considered  the  matter,  the  prayer  for
anticipatory bail is allowed.
7. In the event of arrest or surrender by the petitioners
before the Court concerned within three weeks’ from today,
they are directed to be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as may be imposed by the said Court.

with  regard  to  the  matter  pending  before  it  in  the
